Roommate syndrome is the everyday name for a relationship that has come to feel more like a living arrangement than a partnership. Roommate Syndrome Through a Gottman Lens: Parallel Lives
The Gottman Institute has not studied roommate syndrome specifically. But one way to see it through a Gottman lens could be to look at what Dr. John Gottman calls leading parallel lives.

blocks.x: Most marriages do not end over fighting, Gottman writes. More often, to avoid constant skirmishes, partners distance themselves so much that their friendship and sense of connection are lost. Couples who have settled into that civil distance can look fine from the outside. They may lead parallel lives in the same home, Gottman writes, and go through the motions of togetherness, attending their children’s plays and hosting dinner parties, without feeling connected to each other.

In a study that followed 79 couples for fourteen years, Gottman and Robert Levenson found two waves of divorce. The first came early, within about seven years, and anger in the couples’ conflict discussions predicted it. The second came later, around the time the first child turned fourteen. Those couples were not fighting. They had gone flat with each other. In the lab, they showed very little positive emotion and held back the negative, both in a conflict discussion and in a conversation about an ordinary day.

Gottman called them alienated and avoidant, and their marriages passive and distant. Left to themselves, he said, partners in those marriages tend to blame each other for the distance. A couples therapist can help a couple step out of that pattern, and Gottman was hopeful about them: “These marriages can have a renaissance.”

One woman at a Gottman workshop put it this way: “We got along okay and really loved each other, but I didn’t feel that connected to Kevin. It was like we were roommates who made love.” Helen and Kevin had love and goodwill, Gottman writes. They lacked a sense of shared meaning, which he describes as “creating an inner life together—a culture rich with symbols and rituals.”
